slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by positioning homogeneous geometry as the part of Riemannian geometry where symmetry turns analysis into algebra. The audience should hear that the chapter is not just a catalogue of examples. It gives a method: encode the metric at one base point, let the group move it everywhere, and read curvature from Lie algebra data.

slides.label: Lecture Map
slides.notes: Use the map to set expectations for the whole lecture. Homogeneous spaces reduce global metric questions to invariant linear algebra, but the reduction comes with choices: a presentation G over H, a complement to the isotropy algebra, and parameters for invariant inner products. Each later slide revisits one of these choices.

slides.label: Homogeneous Space
slides.notes: The main definition is geometric rather than coordinate-based. A Riemannian manifold is homogeneous when its isometry group can move any point to any other point. Once a base point is fixed, the entire manifold can be viewed as cosets G over H, where H records the symmetries that keep the base point fixed.

slides.label: Invariant Metrics
slides.notes: This slide is the key algebraic translation. Instead of choosing a metric tensor independently at every point, choose an inner product on the tangent model at the base point. The condition that this inner product be invariant under the isotropy representation is exactly what lets it propagate consistently across the orbit.

slides.label: Reductive Split
slides.notes: A reductive decomposition is a controlled way to identify tangent vectors with Lie algebra directions. The complement m should be preserved by the isotropy action, so brackets with h do not push m out of the tangent model. This is a useful bookkeeping device, not merely a notational convenience.

slides.label: Metric Parameters
slides.notes: Many homogeneous examples become finite-dimensional because the isotropy representation splits into irreducible pieces. On inequivalent summands, an invariant metric often scales each block by a positive parameter. The Einstein equation then becomes a system of algebraic equations in those scale parameters.

slides.label: Curvature From Brackets
slides.notes: The important message is that curvature still measures noncommuting directions, but on a homogeneous space the noncommutation is recorded by Lie brackets. Connection and curvature formulas can be assembled from the metric and the bracket table. This is why homogeneous Einstein geometry is computationally tangible.

slides.label: Nomizu Pipeline
slides.notes: Present this as a practical workflow rather than as a single memorized formula. Start with a Lie algebra presentation, choose the tangent complement, choose an invariant inner product, compute the connection operator, then contract curvature to Ricci. Every arrow is algebraic once the homogeneous data are fixed.

slides.label: Einstein Algebra
slides.notes: The Einstein condition compares two invariant bilinear forms on the same tangent model. Because both sides are invariant, it is enough to check the equation at the base point. For parametrized metrics this usually produces polynomial or rational equations, together with the positivity restrictions on the metric parameters.

slides.label: Symmetric Spaces
slides.notes: Symmetric spaces are the cleanest subclass because there is an involution that reverses tangent directions at each point. Algebraically, this forces the bracket of two tangent directions back into the isotropy algebra. That extra bracket structure simplifies curvature and explains why symmetric spaces are standard reservoirs of Einstein metrics.

slides.label: Model Gallery
slides.notes: Treat this slide as a taxonomy, not as a list to memorize. Each model has the same organizing pattern: a transitive group, an isotropy group, and a small tangent representation. The point is to compare how much freedom the invariant metric has before the Einstein equation is imposed.

slides.label: Isotropy Irreducible
slides.notes: This is one of the fastest routes to examples. If the isotropy representation is irreducible, Schur-style reasoning says that invariant symmetric forms have very little room to vary. Under the usual hypotheses this makes an invariant metric automatically Einstein up to scale, which is why representation theory is so efficient here.

slides.label: Normal Homogeneous Metrics
slides.notes: A normal homogeneous metric is built from a group-level inner product, often coming from an Ad-invariant form. This makes geodesic and curvature calculations especially structured. It is useful to emphasize that normal homogeneous is stronger than homogeneous, so it gives convenient examples but not the full landscape.

slides.label: Worked Algebra
slides.notes: Use the two-block model as a board calculation template. The constants in the Ricci expressions stand for bracket contributions between summands, while the variables are metric scales. The Einstein condition asks for the two normalized Ricci values to agree, producing a concrete algebraic constraint.

slides.label: Failure Modes
slides.notes: The chapter is also teaching what can go wrong. A metric may be invariant but not Einstein, a complement may be poorly adapted to the isotropy action, or a parameter choice may leave the positive cone. Naming these failures helps students avoid thinking that symmetry alone solves the Einstein equation.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the central reduction. Homogeneity replaces a global differential problem by invariant algebra at a base point, and symmetric spaces are the most rigid version of that reduction. The key takeaway is that homogeneous Einstein metrics are found by balancing representation-theoretic metric freedom against bracket-driven Ricci curvature.
